rotation we may write

$$
c_{0},c_{1},\dots ,c_{8}=0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,1,
\tag{*}
$$

i.e. $W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B$ round the table.  In $(*)$

$$
s_{i}=1\iff i=1,3,5 ,\qquad s_{i}=2\ {\rm otherwise},
$$

so the three $s_{i}=1$ men see four black hats.  They are the three
isolated black hats

$$
W\,B\,W,
$$

the three men $1,3,5$ in $(*)$, and the remaining two black hats form
the unique $BB$ block $7\!-\!8$.  The four white hats are isolated.

Let $V_{i}$ be the six hats seen by $i$.  With $s_{j}\in\{1,2\}$ the
word $(*)$ is the only circular $5\!-\!4$ word and, up to rotation,
the only word which is compatible with the two successive universal
‘No’s.  The $WW$ type is killed by the second ‘No’ : a $WW$ block
forces the neighbour of the block to have a forced hat already after
the first round.

For $i$ with $s_{i}=1$ the three completions of the unseen triple
$(c_{i-1},c_{i},c_{i+1})$ with $c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1}=1$ are
$(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)$.  The two completions different from
$(0,1,0)$ make the neighbour of $i$ know his hat already on the second
call, contrary to the second ‘No’.  Hence the second ‘No’ eliminates
the two spurious completions and $c_{i}=1$ is forced.  The three
$s_{i}=1$ men are therefore the only men who acquire a forced colour
on the third call; they are the three isolated black men $W B W$,
the three $k_{i}=4$ men in $(*)$.

In the normalisation $(*)$ these are the men $1,3,5$,
$W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B$, and any rotation or mirror of $(*)$ is the
same essentially unique distribution.  Up to rotation the hat
distribution is one adjacent black pair and three isolated blacks,
the four whites being isolated, e.g. $B\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W$.

In particular the three isolated black hats are the three men who can
say “Yes’’ on the third announcement.  With the usual
identification up to rotation the five positions $1,2,3,4,5$ have a
unique six-hat view in the $C_{9}$-orbit of $(*)$; three of them are
the three black $W B W$ men above and the two white $B W B$ men $2,4$
are the white hats whose view is also unique.  This is the five
identifiable views usually quoted in the literature, the essentially
new knowledge being the three $W B W$ black hats.  Neglecting the two
forced white views this is the customary three-Yes statement of the
puzzle. ∎

6.text:
On the symbols

$$c_{i}=1\;{\rm B},\qquad c_{i}=0\;{\rm W},\qquad\sum_{i}c_{i}=5,
\qquad s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1},\qquad 
k_{i}=5-s_{i}$$

the first ``No'' is

$$k_{i}\ne2,5\iff s_{i}\ne0,3\iff1\le s_{i}\le2\qquad0\le i<9, $$

i.e. no $000$ and no $111$ on three consecutive seats.  Hence

$$\sum s_{i}=3\sum c_{i}=15,\qquad 
\#\{s_{i}=1\}=3,\qquad\#\{s_{i}=2\}=6,
\tag{1}
$$

and $k_{i}=4$ for the three $s_{i}=1$ seats and $k_{i}=3$ for the
remaining six.  Up to rotation and reflexion the $5\!-\!4$ circular
word with $s_{i}\in\{1,2\}$ is the almost alternating word.  Modulo
rotation we may write it as

$$W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\tag{2}$$

and every cyclic permutation of (2).  In particular there is exactly
one adjacent black pair, the four white hats are isolated and the three
remaining black hats are isolated $W B W$.  With the normalisation (2)

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
i      &0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\ \hline
c_{i} &0&1&0&1&0&1&0&1&1\\
s_{i}&2&1&2&1&2&1&2&2&2
\end{array}
$$

so that $s_{i}=1$ i.e. $k_{i}=4$ exactly on the three isolated
black seats $1,3,5$, the $W B W$ seats.  Put

$$V_{i}=\bigl(c_{i+2},c_{i+3},c_{i+4},c_{i+5},c_{i+6},c_{i+7}\bigr) .
$$

For the word (2)

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{0}&=V_{7}=W B W B W B ,\\
V_{6}&=V_{8}= B W B W B W ,\\
V_{1}&=B W B W B B ,\;V_{2}=W B W B B W ,\\
V_{3}&=B W B B W B ,\;V_{4}=W B B W B W ,\;V_{5}=B B W B W B ,
\end{aligned}
$$
i.e. $V_{0}\equiv V_{7}$ and $V_{6}\equiv V_{8}$ and the five views
$V_{1},V_{2},V_{3},V_{4},V_{5}$ are distinct.  Hence on the set
$\mathcal S_{2}$ of worlds which survive the two common ``No''s, which
up to rotation is the nine rotations of (2), a seat whose view is
$V_{1},\dots ,V_{5}$ has a unique $d=s-k\pmod 9$ and therefore a
unique hat; a seat whose view is $V_{0}\equiv V_{7}$ or
$V_{6}\equiv V_{8}$ has the two completions $d=0,7$ resp. $d=6,8$ and
is still ambiguous.

In the actual realisation (2) the five seats whose view is
uniquely determined are

* the three isolated black seats $1,3,5$,
  $W\,B\,W$, $s_{i}=1$, $k_{i}=4$, and
* the two white seats $2,4$ which sit between two isolated blacks,
  $B\,W\,B$,

and they are the five seats which can name their hat on the third
announcement.  In the usual formulation the new information is the
three $W B W$ men, i.e. the three isolated black hats; they are the
three who learn that they are black.  Up to rotation this is the
customary $B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W$, e.g.

$B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W\; \equiv\; W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B,$

the unique $5\!-\!4$ necklace with one $BB$ block, three isolated
$B$'s and four isolated $W$'s, no $BBB$ and no $WWW$.  The three
isolated $B$'s are the three $s_{i}=1$, $k_{i}=4$ $W B W$ men which are
normally quoted as the three ``Yes'' answers; with the two white
$B W B$ men who become forced as well the number of affirmative
answers in the realisation is the five uniquely identifiable seats,
three black and two white, $1,2,3,4,5$ in the normalisation above.
Discarding the two white answers this is the familiar three black
``Yes'' statement, the three $W B W$ men, the essentially unique
distribution being the one $BB$ pair with the remaining three blacks
isolated between whites.  This is the distribution usually written as
$B B W B W B W B W$ up to rotation. ∎

10.text:
The six hats which are not seen by $i$ are $c_{i-1},c_{i},c_{i+1}$ and we put
$c_{i}=1$ for $B$, $c_{i}=0$ for $W$,
$$
s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1},\qquad k_{i}=5-s_{i},
$$
$k_{i}$ being the number of black hats which $i$ sees.  $i$ would know his
own hat on the first call iff $k_{i}=2$ or $k_{i}=5$, i.e. iff
$s_{i}=0$ or $s_{i}=3$.  Hence after the first

$${\rm No}\qquad 1\le s_{i}\le 2\qquad 0\le i<9,
\tag{1}
$$

in particular no three consecutive hats are monochromatic.  Summation
gives
$\sum_{i}s_{i}=3\sum_{i}c_{i}=15$, whence with $a$ the number of
$i$ with $s_{i}=1$

$a+2(9-a)=15$, $a=3$, i.e.

$$
\#\{s_{i}=1\}=3,\qquad\#\{s_{i}=2\}=6,
$$

and $k_{i}=4$ for the three $s_{i}=1$ men and $k_{i}=3$ for the
other six.  Up to rotation and reflexion the only $5\!-\!4$ circular
word with no $000$ and no $111$ and with three triples of weight one is

$$
0\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,1 ,
$$

i.e. up to rotation

$$
W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\equiv B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W .
\tag{2}
$$

In the normalisation

$$
c_{0}=0,c_{1}=1,c_{2}=0,c_{3}=1,c_{4}=0,c_{5}=1,c_{6}=0,c_{7}=1,c_{8}=1
$$

$$
s_{i}=1\iff i=1,3,5,\qquad s_{i}=2\ {\rm otherwise},
$$

so that $k_{i}=4$ for $i=1,3,5$ and $k_{i}=3$ for the remaining six.
The three $s_{i}=1$ windows are the three $W\,B\,W$ triples.  For a
man with $s_{i}=1$ the three completions of the triple
$c_{i-1},c_{i},c_{i+1}$ of weight one are
$(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)$.  The two completions $(1,0,0)$ and
$(0,0,1)$ make the two neighbours of $i$ have a forced hat already
after the first round and are therefore eliminated by the first
${\rm No}$.  After the second ${\rm No}$ the only completion which is
still compatible with the common knowledge that every $s_{j}\in\{1,2\}$
and that nobody could decide after the first round is the central one

$$
c_{i-1}=c_{i+1}=0,\qquad c_{i}=1,
$$

i.e. the $W\,B\,W$ neighbourhood.  Hence the three men whose own
triple is of weight one, the three isolated black hats
$c_{i}=1$ with $c_{i-1}=c_{i+1}=0$, are the only ones for whom the
common knowledge of the first two ${\rm No}$’s makes the colour of
$c_{i}$ common knowledge.  In the normalisation above they are
$i=1,3,5$.  They see four black hats and they now know that their two
neighbours are white and therefore that their own hat is black.

Up to rotation this is the unique distribution compatible with two
successive ${\rm No}$’s and a ${\rm Yes}$ on the third call, viz. four
isolated white hats, three isolated black hats $W\,B\,W$ and one
adjacent black pair.  In the usual cyclic notation this is

$$
B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W,
$$

and any rotation of it, e.g. $W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B$.  The three
$W\,B\,W$ men, the three isolated black hats, are the three persons
who can say ${\rm Yes}$ on the third call; the two black hats of the
unique $BB$ block and the four white hats stay undecided at this
stage.  In particular the three affirmative answers are the three
isolated $W\,B\,W$ black hats, the conventional three-Yes statement.
The five black-hat wearers are the five persons whose six-hat view is
unique up to rotation in the $C_{2}$-orbit of the word (2); this is the
five-black statement often quoted. ∎

8.text:
With $c_{i}=1$ for $B$ and $0$ for $W$ put

$$s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1},\qquad v_{i}=5-s_{i}, $$

$v_{i}$ being the number of black hats seen by $i$.  On the first
announcement $v_{i}\ne2,5$, i.e.

$$1\le s_{i}\le2\qquad0\le i<9 ,$$

and

$$\sum_{i}s_{i}=3\sum_{i}c_{i}=15.$$

Hence with $a$ the number of triples of weight $1$ and $b$ the number of
triples of weight $2$

$$a+b=9,\qquad a+2b=15,$$

so that $a=3$ and $b=6$.  In particular no three consecutive hats are
$000$ and no three consecutive hats are $111$ and after the first

*``No'' every three consecutive hats contain one or two black hats;
three triples contain one black hat and six triples contain two black
hats.  $v_{i}=4$ for the three $s_{i}=1$ men and $v_{i}=3$ for the six
$s_{i}=2$ men.*

Up to rotation and reflexion the only $5\!-\!4$ circular word with no
$000$, no $111$ and with three weight $1$ windows is the almost
alternating word.  With the usual normalisation

$$W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\pmod 9,$$

i.e. in cyclic order

$$0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,1,$$

one adjacent $BB$–block and the other three black hats isolated in
$W B W$.  In the normalisation

$${\rm
c_{0}=0,\;c_{1}=1,\;c_{2}=0,\;c_{3}=1,\;c_{4}=0,\;c_{5}=1,\;
c_{6}=0,\;c_{7}=1,\;c_{8}=1 }$$

we have

$$s_{i}=1\iff i\equiv1,3,5\pmod 9, $$

the three isolated $W B W$ triples, and $s_{i}=2$ otherwise.  The
four white hats are isolated, the black runs are $1,1,1,2$, and, up to
rotation, this is the unique $5\!-\!4$ word with $s_{i}\in\{1,2\}$.

Let $i$ be an isolated black, $s_{i}=1$.  The three completions of the
triple $c_{i-1},c_{i},c_{i+1}$ of weight one are $100,010,001$.
The two completions $100$ and $001$ create a $111$ window at
$i\pm1$ and are therefore incompatible with $s_{j}\in\{1,2\}\;\forall
j$.  The completion $010$ is the only one which is compatible with the
second common “No’’.  Hence after the second common “No’’ a man who sees
four black hats knows that his two neighbours are white and that he
himself is black.  The three men who sit on the three $W B W$ triples,
the three $s_{i}=1$ men, are the first men who can be sure of their own
colour.  In the normalisation above they are $c_{1},c_{3},c_{5}$,
the three isolated black hats; the $BB$–block is $c_{7}c_{8}$.  Any
cyclic permutation or mirror image of

$$B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W$$

is the same distribution.  In particular the three isolated black
hats are the three new “Yes’’ answers on the third announcement; the
six remaining seats stay undecided on the third round in the usual
statement of the puzzle.  Up to the obvious rotation the six–hat view
is unique for five seats, the three isolated blacks $c_{1},c_{3},c_{5}$
and the two whites $c_{0},c_{2}$ which flank them, i.e. five men, three
black and two white, have a unique view in the $9$–orbit.  This is the
conventional three–black–hat, five–unique–view formulation of the
puzzle. ∎

12.text:
The six hats which $i$ can see are the six hats which are not
$i-1,i,i+1$.  Put $c_{i}=1$ for $B$ and $c_{i}=0$ for $W$ and

$$
s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1},\qquad v_{i}=5-s_{i}
$$

$v_{i}$ is the number of black hats seen by $i$.  After the first
``No''

$$
v_{i}\ne 2,5\iff s_{i}\ne0,3\iff1\le s_{i}\le2,
\tag{1}
$$

hence no three consecutive hats are $000$ or $111$ and

$$
\sum_{i}s_{i}=3\sum_{i}c_{i}=15,
\qquad
\#\{s_{i}=1\}=3,\;\#\{s_{i}=2\}=6,
$$

so that $v_{i}=4$ for the three $s_{i}=1$ men and $v_{i}=3$ for the
six $s_{i}=2$ men.  In particular a word which can survive the first
announcement is a circular $5\!-\!4$ word with no run $000$ and no run
$111$.

Let $S$ be the set of such words.  Put $S_{2}\subset S$ for the words
for which no man can force his own colour from his six hat view and
from (1).  A word of $S$ with a $WW$ run has

$$
r_{1}=r_{0}\ge 3,\qquad \sum_{0}^{r_{0}-1}w_{j}=4,
$$

and $r_{0}=3$ gives the $WW$–type
$2,2,1$ for the black runs and $2,1,1$ for the white runs.  For that
type the man who sees the $WW$ block has the three unseen hats
$c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1}=1$ with three admissible completions and the
two spurious completions force a neighbour to know his hat already
after the first announcement.  Hence every $WW$–word is eliminated by
the second ``No''.  With no $WW$ run we have $r_{0}=r_{1}=4$ and,
$\sum w_{j}=4$, $w_{j}=1\;\forall j$, so that in $S_{2}$

* the four white hats are isolated,
* $r_{1}=4$, $\sum b_{j}=5$ gives the black run lengths $2,1,1,1$,
* there is exactly one $BB$ adjacency and no $WW$ adjacency.

Up to rotation and reflexion this is the almost alternating neck
lace

$$
W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B ,
\tag{2}
$$

i.e. in the normalisation

$$
c_{0}=0,\;c_{1}=1,\;c_{2}=0,\;c_{3}=1,\;c_{4}=0,\;c_{5}=1,\;
c_{6}=0,\;c_{7}=1,\;c_{8}=1,
$$

and every rotation of (2) is the same word.  In (2)

$$
s_{i}=1\iff i=1,3,5 ,\qquad s_{i}=2\ {\rm otherwise},
$$

so that $i=1,3,5$ are the three $W B W$ isolated blacks, $k_{i}=4$,
and $i=2,4,6$ are the three whites $B W B$ which sit between two
isolated blacks.  For a man $i$ let ${\cal W}_{i}\subset S_{2}$ be the
words of $S_{2}$ which agree with the six hats seen by $i$.  For the
three isolated blacks $i=1,3,5$ the view contains the $BB$ block
$7\!-\!8$, whence the three completions of the hidden triple
$c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1}=1$,

$$
(1,0,0),\;(0,1,0),\;(0,0,1),
$$

are reduced to the single completion $(0,1,0)$ by the requirement
``no $WW$ and exactly one $BB$''.  Hence

$$
c_{i}=1\qquad i=1,3,5,
$$

is common knowledge after the two ``No''s.  The two white neighbours
of the first two isolated blacks,

$$
i=2\ {\rm with}\ (c_{1},c_{2},c_{3})=(1,0,1),\qquad
i=4\ {\rm with}\ (c_{3},c_{4},c_{5})=(1,0,1),
$$

are forced to be white by the same $WW$/$BB$ elimination, whereas
the white $i=6$ which sits immediately before the $BB$ block and the
white $i=0$ which sits immediately after it still have the two
$ S_{2}$–completions

$$
(c_{5},c_{6},c_{7})=(1,0,1)\leftrightarrow(1,1,0),\qquad
(c_{8},c_{0},c_{1})=(1,0,1)\leftrightarrow(0,1,1),
$$

and the two $BB$–men $i=7,8$ still have the two completions
$(c_{6},c_{7},c_{8})=(0,1,1)\leftrightarrow(1,0,1)$.  Hence after the
common knowledge of the two successive ``No''s the five men

$$
i=1,2,3,4,5
$$

have a unique six-hat view in $S_{2}$: $i=1,3,5$ know that they are
the three isolated black hats $W B W$ and $i=2,4$ know that they are
the two whites $B W B$ which flank the first two isolated blacks.
Up to rotation these are the three $W B W$ men; in the usual
statement they are quoted as the three isolated black hats which are
the first to know that they are black.  The six remaining men, the
$BB$ pair $7\!-\!8$ and the white $0$ and $6$, still have two
compatible rotations of (2).

In particular the essentially unique distribution compatible with two
universal ``No''s and a ``Yes'' on the third question is the one $BB$
pair with the other three blacks isolated by the four whites, e.g.

$$
B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W
$$

clockwise, which is (2) up to rotation.  The three $W B W$ positions
are the three black hats which become common knowledge on the third
call; with the conventional counting of the five men whose six-hat
view is uniquely determined in $S_{2}$ this is five ``Yes'' answers,
three black and two white, the three black answers being the
customary three-Yes statement.  Any rotation or reflexion of
$W B W B W B W B B$ is the same necklace. ∎

public_text.7:
I’d back the 3-Yes conclusion, and I think the key is not to count every seat that has a unique row in the full necklace.

Let \(h_i=1\) for black and \(h_i=0\) for white, and put \(s_i=h_{i-1}+h_i+h_{i+1}\). The first “No” says nobody initially sees a forced color, so \(s_i\in\{1,2\}\) for every \(i\). Summing gives exactly three indices with \(s_i=1\). The second “No” eliminates the competing type where the two white hats form a \(WW\) block; what survives, up to rotation, is the one-\(BB\)-block type, e.g. \(BWBWBBWBW\). So I agree with Colleagues 2, 3, 6, 11, and 12 that the distribution is a rotation of \(BWBWBBWBW\).

The mistake in the 5-Yes readings is treating “the full circular pattern is unique up to rotation” as “five particular people know their own hats.” For the three isolated black hats, the local three-window is forced to be \(W B W\): if it were \(B W W\) or \(W W B\), one of the neighbors would have been able to decide earlier, contradicting the second all-“No” round. Those three isolated black-hat wearers therefore know they are black on the third question.

But the two blacks in the \(BB\) pair and the whites do not get a similarly forced answer at their own seat. For a black in the \(BB\) pair, the adjacent pair could be shifted one step relative to his six-hat view while preserving all previous “No” answers; locally his own color is still not forced. The same applies to the neighboring whites. Colleague 1’s count of “five black hats” counts hats in the global pattern, not people who can identify their own hat. Colleague 4’s “five identifiable views” similarly counts rotations/reflections of the whole necklace as if the observer knew the global orientation, which is exactly what is not given by the first two rounds.

Also, Colleagues 7, 9, and 14’s distribution \(BWBWBBWWB\) contains a \(WW\) block and should not survive the second round derivation. So the 5-Yes camp is both split and overcounting.

Thus my answer is: exactly **3** people reply “Yes,” and the hats are, up to rotation,

\[
B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W\,B\,W.
\]

The three who say “Yes” are the isolated black-hat wearers, i.e. the three \(W B W\) positions.
public_text.1: I’m still with the 3-Yes solution. The key is that after the second “No” the surviving circular type is the one with a single adjacent BB pair and four isolated whites, e.g. BWBWBBWBW up to rotation/reflection. The only people whose own colour is forced by their own view are the three isolated black hats, the W-B-W positions. Someone who can see the BB pair can locate where that pair is, but that does not by itself force their own colour unless they are one of those three isolated black hats; the white-hatted seats outside the pair still have a consistent completion consistent with the first two universal “No”s. So Colleague 4’s count of five overcounts those outside the forced W-B-W seats. Also, the 5-Yes variants containing a WW block, such as BWBWBBWWB, cannot survive the second “No” because that WW block is exactly the kind of local ambiguity that would have produced a “Yes” on round 2. Thus the consistent answer is: exactly 3 people replied “Yes,” with distribution BWBWBBWBW clockwise, up to rotation/reflection.
public_text.5:
I’m still in the 3-yes camp. The first “No” gives \(s_i \in \{1,2\}\) for every seat, and summing forces exactly three positions with \(s_i=1\). The second “No” then eliminates the two-\(BB\)/one-\(WW\) type; what survives is the almost-alternating circular pattern with one \(BB\) block and four isolated whites, e.g. \(BWBWBBWBW\) up to rotation/reflection.

The 5-yes answers seem to overcount by treating any six-hat block that is unique in a fixed representative as if the wearer knows the rotation. The deduction available after round 2 only forces the three isolated \(B\)’s: for those \(s_i=1\) people, the alternative placements of the single black in their hidden triple would have made a neighbor certain on round 2. For the adjacent \(BB\) pair and the remaining whites, shifting the \(BB\) block one step still gives the same visible six-hat string and preserves all previous “No”s, so their own color is not forced. In particular \(BWBWBBWWB\) contains a \(WW\) block, which is exactly the type ruled out by the second round. So the consistent answer is 3 “Yes,” with \(BWBWBBWBW\) up to rotation.
public_text.9:
I’d keep the answer at **3 people replied “Yes”**, with the hats distributed up to rotation as

**B W B W B B W B W**.

The first “No” gives the standard condition: for every seat \(i\), the three-hat block \(c_{i-1},c_i,c_{i+1}\) has sum \(1\) or \(2\). Summing around the circle gives exactly three seats with sum \(1\), and after the second “No” the only surviving circular type is the almost-alternating one with a single adjacent \(BB\) pair and all whites isolated. In that type, the three sum-\(1\) seats are precisely the three isolated black hats, the ones sitting in a \(W-B-W\) neighborhood.

For those three, the unseen triple contains exactly one black, and the two alternative placements would force a neighbouring person to have known by the second round; since the second round was another unanimous “No,” those alternatives are eliminated. So those three can now say “Yes.”

The issue with the 5-answer or 4-answer positions is that they are counting people whose six-hat visible block happens to be unique in the final completed necklace. But uniqueness of a visible block in an already-known global arrangement is not the same as having enough public information at the third question to force one’s own hat. The adjacent \(BB\) wearers and the whites usually counted by the larger answers still have a locally consistent completion after the first two “No”s, so they cannot yet answer “Yes.” Thus I think exactly the three isolated black-hat wearers reply “Yes,” with distribution **BWBWBBWBW** up to rotation.
public_text.14:
I agree with the Type A elimination that several people have given: after the first “No,” no three consecutive hats can be monochromatic; after the second “No,” the only surviving circular pattern is one adjacent \(BB\) block and four isolated whites, e.g.  
\[
W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B
\]
which is the same as C1’s \(B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W\) up to rotation.

Where I think C1/C5/C13 overcount is in the third-round yes-set. In that pattern, the two blacks inside the \(BB\) block cannot both deduce their color: moving the \(BB\) block one seat left or right gives another Type A assignment with the same six visible hats for each of them, so their own color is not forced. The remaining whites also still have two Type A completions consistent with their six-hat view and the two universal “No” answers.

The only seats where the centered triple is actually forced are the three isolated black hats, i.e. the \(W\!-\!B\!-\!W\) centers. For such a person, the second “No” rules out the spurious triples with the black at an end, because those would have made a neighbor know on round 2. Hence exactly the three isolated black-hat wearers can answer “Yes.”

So my current answer is: **3 people replied “Yes,” with distribution \(W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\)** up to rotation, e.g. \(B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W\,B\,W\).
public_text.13:
I think the three-Yes reading is still the most stable. The first “No” rules out any 3-window with 0 or 3 black hats. The second “No” removes the patterns with an adjacent WW block, because the person next to that block can force his own hat on the second round, and it leaves exactly the circular type with one adjacent BB pair and all other black hats isolated by single whites. Up to rotation, that is:

**B B W B W B W B W**  
(or equivalently **B W B W B W B B W**).

On the third question, only the three isolated black hats can be certain. They are the **W B W** positions: for such a person the unseen triple has sum 1, and the only completion compatible with the two earlier “No”s and with the middle being black is **W B W**; the other two sum-1 completions would have made a neighbor know earlier. The two black hats in the BB block cannot distinguish the two possible placements of that block, so they do not know. The whites also do not know: their own color is still compatible with rotating the unique BB block one step while preserving their six visible hats and all previous “No”s.

The five-Yes claims either use something like **B W B W B B W W B**, which contains a WW block and is eliminated by the second “No”, or they count people merely because their view is unique in an externally fixed orbit. But uniqueness of a view from the outside is not the same as the simultaneous public-announcement information available to that person.

So I would answer: **3 people replied “Yes”**, with the distribution, up to rotation, **B B W B W B W B W** — one adjacent BB pair and three isolated black hats.

With $c_{i}=1$ for black and $0$ for white put

$$s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1}\qquad 0\le i<9,
\qquad\sum c_{i}=5 .$$

The number of black hats seen by $i$ is $5-s_{i}$.  $i$ would know his
own hat on the first call iff $5-s_{i}=5$ or $5-s_{i}=2$, i.e. iff
$s_{i}=0$ or $s_{i}=3$.  The first universal No is therefore

$$1\le s_{i}\le 2\qquad\forall i , $$

i.e. no $000$ and no $111$ occurs in the circular word.  In
particular

$$\sum_{i}s_{i}=3\sum_{i}c_{i}=15,\qquad 
s_{i}\in\{1,2\}, $$

so that with $x=\#\{s_{i}=1\}$

$$x+2(9-x)=15\iff x=3.$$
Hence after the first No
$$s_{i}=1\ {\rm for\ three\ }i,\qquad s_{i}=2\ {\rm for\ the\ six\ }i,$$
$k_{i}=5-s_{i}=4$ for the three $s_{i}=1$ men and $k_{i}=3$ for the
six $s_{i}=2$ men.  Up to rotation and reflexion the only
$5\!-\!4$ circular word with no $000$ and no $111$ and with three
triples of weight $1$ is the almost alternating word

$$0\,1\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\qquad{\rm mod}\;9, $$

i.e. in the usual notation

$$W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B,$$

and any rotation of it.  In the normalisation

$$c_{0}=c_{1}=1,\;c_{3}=c_{5}=c_{7}=1,\;c_{2}=c_{4}=c_{6}=c_{8}=0, $$

we have

$$s_{0}=s_{1}=s_{2}=s_{4}=s_{6}=s_{8}=2,\qquad
s_{3}=s_{5}=s_{7}=1, $$

so that the three $s_{i}=1$ positions are the three isolated black
hats

$$W\,B\,W\qquad i=3,5,7 .$$

For an isolated black $i$ we have $k_{i}=4$ and $s_{i}=1$.  Up to the
common knowledge $s_{j}\in\{1,2\}\;\forall j$ the three admissible
completions of the hidden triple $c_{i-1},c_{i},c_{i+1}$ with sum $1$
are $(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)$.  The two completions
$(1,0,0)$ and $(0,0,1)$ force the neighbour of $i$ to have a
$111$ or a $000$ three-window and therefore to know his own hat
already after the first announcement.  Since the second announcement
is again a universal No those two completions are eliminated by the
common knowledge and the only admissible completion which survives
the two successive No’s is

$$c_{i-1}=0,\;c_{i}=1,\;c_{i+1}=0, $$

i.e. $i$ is the unique black of a $W\,B\,W$ triple.  The three men
with $s_{i}=1$ are therefore the only men who can be sure of the
colour of their own hat after the two No’s.  They are the three
isolated black hats $W\,B\,W$.  In the normalisation above they are
$i=3,5,7$, the three black hats which are flanked by white hats on
both sides; the remaining two black hats form the unique $BB$ block
and the four white hats are isolated.  Up to rotation this is

$$B\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W,$$

the one adjacent $BB$ pair and three isolated $B$’s, four isolated
$W$’s, no $BBB$ and no $WWW$.  This is the essentially unique
$5\!-\!4$ circular word compatible with two successive universal
No’s.  The three isolated $B$’s are the new knowledge on the third
call; in the usual counting they are the three Yes answers.  The
six-hat view of the two white neighbours of the $BB$ block is also
uniquely determined in the $9$-orbit, so that in the customary
phrasing five persons, the three isolated blacks and the two whites
flanking the $BB$ block, have a uniquely determined six-hat view,
three of them being the new black knowledge quoted in the literature.
∎

For $c_{i}=1$ for black, $0$ for white put

$$s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1},\qquad v_{i}=5-s_{i}$$

for the number of black hats seen by $i$.  After the first ``No''

$$v_{i}\ne 2,5\iff s_{i}\ne0,3\iff 1\le s_{i}\le 2\qquad
0\le i<9                            $$

hence no three consecutive hats are monochromatic.  With
$\sum s_{i}=3\sum c_{i}=15$

$$a+\!2b=15,\qquad a+b=9\iff a=3,\;b=6, $$

so after the first announcement

* $s_{i}=1$ for three $i$ and $s_{i}=2$ for the other six,
* $v_{i}=4$ for the three $s_{i}=1$ men and $v_{i}=3$ for the six
$s_{i}=2$ men.

In particular $\sum c_{i}c_{i+1}=5$, i.e. there is exactly one
adjacent $BB$ pair and no $BBB$ and no $WWW$ occurs.  Up to rotation
and reflexion the $5\!-\!4$ circular word with $s_{i}\in\{1,2\}$ is
unique.  With the normalisation

\begin{equation*}
c_{0}=0,\;c_{1}=1,\;c_{2}=0,\;c_{3}=1,\;c_{4}=0,\;c_{5}=1,\;
c_{6}=0,\;c_{7}=1,\;c_{8}=1
\end{equation*}

i.e. up to rotation

$$W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\equiv
B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W $$

we have

$$s_{i}=1\;{\rm for}\;i=1,3,5,\qquad s_{i}=2\;{\rm otherwise}, $$

so that the three $s_{i}=1$ triples are the three isolated
$W\,B\,W$ triples

$$c_{0}c_{1}c_{2}=0\,1\,0,\qquad c_{2}c_{3}c_{4}=0\,1\,0,
\qquad c_{4}c_{5}c_{6}=0\,1\,0, $$

and the only adjacent black pair is $c_{7}c_{8}=1\,1$.  The four
white hats are isolated and the three remaining black hats are
isolated by white hats on both sides.  This is the unique $5\!-\!4$
necklace with no $000$ and no $111$.  Any rotation of it, e.g.
$B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W$, is the same configuration.

Put $W_{i}$ for the six hats seen by $i$.  After the two universal
``No''s a world $w$ is admissible iff $s_{j}(w)\in\{1,2\}$ for every
$j$ and for every $j$ there is a $w'\in W_{1}$ indistinguishable from
$w$ for $j$ with $c_{j}(w')\ne c_{j}(w)$.  For the word above the three
men with $s_{i}=1$ are the three $W\,B\,W$ men.  For one of them,
say $i=1$, the six hats seen are $c_{3}\dots c_{8}=1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,1$.
The completions of the unknown triple $c_{0}c_{1}c_{2}$ with
$c_{0}+c_{1}+c_{2}=1$ and $s_{j}\in\{1,2\}\;\forall j$ are

$$(0,1,0)\quad{\rm and}\quad(0,0,1),$$

the completion $(1,0,0)$ being excluded by $s_{8}=3$.  The second
completion is eliminated by the common knowledge that the second
announcement was a universal No.  The same elimination occurs for
$i=3$ and $i=5$.  Hence after the two Nos the three $s_{i}=1$ men,
the three isolated black hats, know that their two neighbours are
white and therefore that they themselves are black.  No white man
has a unique completion for his own hat; the two whites which flank
the unique $BB$ block still have the two essentially indistinguishable
six-hat views $B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W$ and $W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B$.

Consequently on the third announcement the only persons who can be
certain of the colour of their own hat are the three isolated black
hats, the three $W\,B\,W$ positions.  In the normalisation above they
are the persons $1,3,5$, i.e. up to rotation the three $B$’s which sit
between two $W$’s.  In the usual formulation this is phrased as the
three isolated black hats becoming certain on the third round; the
five black hats $1,3,5,7,8$ are the forced black hats of the unique
$5\!-\!4$ necklace, the three $W\,B\,W$ men being the new knowledge on
the third call.  Up to rotation and reflection this is the
$B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W$ distribution, i.e. $W B W B W B W B B$, the
unique essentially unique solution. ∎

Write $c_{i}=1$ for $B$, $c_{i}=0$ for $W$ and put

$$
s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1}\qquad 0\le s_{i}\le 3,
\qquad k_{i}=5-s_{i}
$$

for the number of black hats seen by $i$.  $i$ knows his own hat on the
first call iff $k_{i}=2$ or $k_{i}=5$, i.e. iff $s_{i}=0$ or $s_{i}=3$.
Hence after the first common $No$

$$
s_{i}\in\{1,2\},\qquad 0\le i<9,\tag{1}
$$

and in particular no $000$ and no $111$ occurs on the circle.  Now

$$
\sum_{i}s_{i}=3\sum_{i}c_{i}=15,
$$

so with $a$ the number of $i$ with $s_{i}=1$ and $b$ the number with
$s_{i}=2$,

$$
a+b=9,\qquad a+2b=15\iff a=3,\;b=6 .
$$

Thus after the first $No$

* $s_{i}=1$ for three $i$ and $s_{i}=2$ for the other six,
* $k_{i}=4$ for the three $s_{i}=1$ men and $k_{i}=3$ for the six
$s_{i}=2$ men.

Let $V_{i}$ be the six hats seen by $i$.  After the first $No$ $i$
knows (1).  After the second common $No$ $i$ knows that every $j$ still
has at least two completions of the invisible triple
$c_{j-1},c_{j},c_{j+1}$ compatible with (1).  Up to rotation and
reflection the only $5\!-\!1,4\!-\!0$ binary necklace with (1) and with
the property

$$
\#\{\,c_{i-1},c_{i},c_{i+1}:c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1}=s_{i},
\;s_{j}\in\{1,2\}\forall j\,\}\ge2\qquad\forall i
$$

is the almost alternating necklace with one $BB$ block and the four
whites isolated.  Modulo rotation we may write

$$
c_{0}c_{1}c_{2}c_{3}c_{4}c_{5}c_{6}c_{7}c_{8}
=1\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,0 ,
$$

i.e. up to rotation

$$
B\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W ,
$$

and any rotation or reflexion of it.  In the normalisation above

$$
s_{i}=1\iff i\equiv3,5,7\pmod 9,\qquad s_{i}=2\ {\rm otherwise},
$$

and the three $s_{i}=1$ positions are the three isolated black hats

$$
W\,B\,W\qquad i=3,5,7 .
$$

For such an $i$ the three completions of the $1$-window are
$100,010,001$.  The completions $100$ and $001$ create a neighbour with
a unique completion of his invisible triple after the first $No$ and
would therefore have forced a $Yes$ on the second call.  The common
knowledge of the second universal $No$ eliminates them and leaves the
single completion

$$
c_{i-1}=0,\;c_{i}=1,\;c_{i+1}=0,
$$

i.e. the familiar $W B W$.  Hence after the two successive universal
$No$’s the three men who sit on an isolated black hat, the three
$W B W$ spots, know with certainty that they wear black.  No other
man can eliminate both colours for his own hat: e.g. for the two
neighbours of the unique $BB$ block the two triples
$(1,0,1)$ and $(0,1,1)$ are both compatible with the common knowledge
of the two $No$’s.

In particular on the third call the three isolated black-hat wearers
are the only ones who can say $Yes$.  Up to rotation they can be taken
as the three $W B W$ men $3,5,7$ in

$$
B\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W,
$$

the unique circular word with five $1$’s, four $0$’s, one adjacent
$BB$ pair, the remaining three blacks isolated by whites and
$s_{i}\in\{1,2\}$ for every $i$.  This is the essentially unique
distribution compatible with two successive $No$’s.  The two white
neighbours of the $BB$ block have a view which is unique up to
rotation of the above necklace; counting distinct six-hat views up to
rotation this is often phrased as five uniquely identifiable seats,
three black and two white, the three new pieces of common knowledge
being the three $W B W$ black hats.  The three black $W B W$ men are
the three persons who actually acquire new knowledge of their own
hat on the third announcement.  Any rotation or mirror of
$BBW BWBWBW$ is the same distribution. ∎

In the notation $c_{i}=1$ for $B$, $c_{i}=0$ for $W$ put
$s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1}$.  The number of black hats seen by $i$
is $5-s_{i}$.  $i$ would know his own hat on the first call iff
$5-s_{i}=2$ or $5-s_{i}=5$, i.e. iff $s_{i}=0$ or $s_{i}=3$.  The first
‘No’ is therefore

$$s_{i}\in\{1,2\}\qquad 0\le i<9 , $$

i.e. no three consecutive hats are monochromatic.  Putting
$a=\#\{s_{i}=1\},\,b=\#\{s_{i}=2\}$,
$a+b=9,\;a+2b=3\cdot5=15$, whence $a=3,\;b=6$.
Hence after the first No

* $s_{i}=1$ for three men and $s_{i}=2$ for six men,
* $5-s_{i}=4$ for the three $s_{i}=1$ men and $5-s_{i}=3$ for the six
$s_{i}=2$ men.

Up to rotation the $5\!-\!4$ circular word with $s_{i}\in\{1,2\}$ and
no $000,111$ is, mod rotation and reflection, the almost alternating
word with the four whites isolated and one $BB$ block.  Modulo
rotation we may write

$$
c_{0},c_{1},\dots ,c_{8}=0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,1,
\tag{*}
$$

i.e. $W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B$ round the table.  In $(*)$

$$
s_{i}=1\iff i=1,3,5 ,\qquad s_{i}=2\ {\rm otherwise},
$$

so the three $s_{i}=1$ men see four black hats.  They are the three
isolated black hats

$$
W\,B\,W,
$$

the three men $1,3,5$ in $(*)$, and the remaining two black hats form
the unique $BB$ block $7\!-\!8$.  The four white hats are isolated.

Let $V_{i}$ be the six hats seen by $i$.  With $s_{j}\in\{1,2\}$ the
word $(*)$ is the only circular $5\!-\!4$ word and, up to rotation,
the only word which is compatible with the two successive universal
‘No’s.  The $WW$ type is killed by the second ‘No’ : a $WW$ block
forces the neighbour of the block to have a forced hat already after
the first round.

For $i$ with $s_{i}=1$ the three completions of the unseen triple
$(c_{i-1},c_{i},c_{i+1})$ with $c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1}=1$ are
$(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)$.  The two completions different from
$(0,1,0)$ make the neighbour of $i$ know his hat already on the second
call, contrary to the second ‘No’.  Hence the second ‘No’ eliminates
the two spurious completions and $c_{i}=1$ is forced.  The three
$s_{i}=1$ men are therefore the only men who acquire a forced colour
on the third call; they are the three isolated black men $W B W$,
the three $k_{i}=4$ men in $(*)$.

In the normalisation $(*)$ these are the men $1,3,5$,
$W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B$, and any rotation or mirror of $(*)$ is the
same essentially unique distribution.  Up to rotation the hat
distribution is one adjacent black pair and three isolated blacks,
the four whites being isolated, e.g. $B\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W$.

In particular the three isolated black hats are the three men who can
say “Yes’’ on the third announcement.  With the usual
identification up to rotation the five positions $1,2,3,4,5$ have a
unique six-hat view in the $C_{9}$-orbit of $(*)$; three of them are
the three black $W B W$ men above and the two white $B W B$ men $2,4$
are the white hats whose view is also unique.  This is the five
identifiable views usually quoted in the literature, the essentially
new knowledge being the three $W B W$ black hats.  Neglecting the two
forced white views this is the customary three-Yes statement of the
puzzle. ∎

The six hats which are not seen by $i$ are $c_{i-1},c_{i},c_{i+1}$ and we put
$c_{i}=1$ for $B$, $c_{i}=0$ for $W$,

gives

$a+2(9-a)=15$, $a=3$, i.e.

$$
\#\{s_{i}=1\}=3,\qquad\#\{s_{i}=2\}=6,
$$

and $k_{i}=4$ for the three $s_{i}=1$ men and $k_{i}=3$ for the
other six.  Up to rotation and reflexion the only $5\!-\!4$ circular

$$
0\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,1 ,

$$

$$

$$
s_{i}=1\iff i=1,3,5,\qquad s_{i}=2\ {\rm otherwise},
$$

so that $k_{i}=4$ for $i=1,3,5$ and $k_{i}=3$ for the remaining six.

man with $s_{i}=1$ the three completions of the triple

after the first round and are therefore eliminated by the first

still compatible with the common knowledge that every $s_{j}\in\{1,2\}$

neighbours are white and therefore that their own hat is black.

Up to rotation this is the unique distribution compatible with two
successive ${\rm No}$’s and a ${\rm Yes}$ on the third call, viz. four
isolated white hats, three isolated black hats $W\,B\,W$ and one
adjacent black pair.  In the usual cyclic notation this is

$$
B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W,
$$

and any rotation of it, e.g. $W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B$.  The three
$W\,B\,W$ men, the three isolated black hats, are the three persons
who can say ${\rm Yes}$ on the third call; the two black hats of the
unique $BB$ block and the four white hats stay undecided at this
stage.  In particular the three affirmative answers are the three
isolated $W\,B\,W$ black hats, the conventional three-Yes statement.
The five black-hat wearers are the five persons whose six-hat view is
unique up to rotation in the $C_{2}$-orbit of the word (2); this is the
five-black statement often quoted. ∎
public_text.8:
With $c_{i}=1$ for $B$ and $0$ for $W$ put

$$s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1},\qquad v_{i}=5-s_{i}, $$

$v_{i}$ being the number of black hats seen by $i$.  On the first
announcement $v_{i}\ne2,5$, i.e.

$$1\le s_{i}\le2\qquad0\le i<9 ,$$

and

$$\sum_{i}s_{i}=3\sum_{i}c_{i}=15.$$

Hence with $a$ the number of triples of weight $1$ and $b$ the number of
triples of weight $2$

$$a+b=9,\qquad a+2b=15,$$

so that $a=3$ and $b=6$.  In particular no three consecutive hats are
$000$ and no three consecutive hats are $111$ and after the first

*``No'' every three consecutive hats contain one or two black hats;
three triples contain one black hat and six triples contain two black
hats.  $v_{i}=4$ for the three $s_{i}=1$ men and $v_{i}=3$ for the six
$s_{i}=2$ men.*

Up to rotation and reflexion the only $5\!-\!4$ circular word with no
$000$, no $111$ and with three weight $1$ windows is the almost
alternating word.  With the usual normalisation

$$W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\pmod 9,$$

i.e. in cyclic order

$$0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,1,$$

one adjacent $BB$–block and the other three black hats isolated in
$W B W$.  In the normalisation

$${\rm
c_{0}=0,\;c_{1}=1,\;c_{2}=0,\;c_{3}=1,\;c_{4}=0,\;c_{5}=1,\;
c_{6}=0,\;c_{7}=1,\;c_{8}=1 }$$

we have

$$s_{i}=1\iff i\equiv1,3,5\pmod 9, $$

the three isolated $W B W$ triples, and $s_{i}=2$ otherwise.  The
four white hats are isolated, the black runs are $1,1,1,2$, and, up to
rotation, this is the unique $5\!-\!4$ word with $s_{i}\in\{1,2\}$.

Let $i$ be an isolated black, $s_{i}=1$.  The three completions of the
triple $c_{i-1},c_{i},c_{i+1}$ of weight one are $100,010,001$.
The two completions $100$ and $001$ create a $111$ window at
$i\pm1$ and are therefore incompatible with $s_{j}\in\{1,2\}\;\forall
j$.  The completion $010$ is the only one which is compatible with the
second common “No’’.  Hence after the second common “No’’ a man who sees
four black hats knows that his two neighbours are white and that he
himself is black.  The three men who sit on the three $W B W$ triples,
the three $s_{i}=1$ men, are the first men who can be sure of their own
colour.  In the normalisation above they are $c_{1},c_{3},c_{5}$,
the three isolated black hats; the $BB$–block is $c_{7}c_{8}$.  Any
cyclic permutation or mirror image of

$$B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W$$

is the same distribution.  In particular the three isolated black
hats are the three new “Yes’’ answers on the third announcement; the
six remaining seats stay undecided on the third round in the usual
statement of the puzzle.  Up to the obvious rotation the six–hat view
is unique for five seats, the three isolated blacks $c_{1},c_{3},c_{5}$
and the two whites $c_{0},c_{2}$ which flank them, i.e. five men, three
black and two white, have a unique view in the $9$–orbit.  This is the
conventional three–black–hat, five–unique–view formulation of the
puzzle. ∎
public_text.12:
The six hats which $i$ can see are the six hats which are not
$i-1,i,i+1$.  Put $c_{i}=1$ for $B$ and $c_{i}=0$ for $W$ and

$$
s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1},\qquad v_{i}=5-s_{i}
$$

$v_{i}$ is the number of black hats seen by $i$.  After the first
``No''

$$
v_{i}\ne 2,5\iff s_{i}\ne0,3\iff1\le s_{i}\le2,
\tag{1}
$$

hence no three consecutive hats are $000$ or $111$ and

$$
\sum_{i}s_{i}=3\sum_{i}c_{i}=15,
\qquad
\#\{s_{i}=1\}=3,\;\#\{s_{i}=2\}=6,
$$

so that $v_{i}=4$ for the three $s_{i}=1$ men and $v_{i}=3$ for the
six $s_{i}=2$ men.  In particular a word which can survive the first
announcement is a circular $5\!-\!4$ word with no run $000$ and no run
$111$.

Let $S$ be the set of such words.  Put $S_{2}\subset S$ for the words
for which no man can force his own colour from his six hat view and
from (1).  A word of $S$ with a $WW$ run has

$$
r_{1}=r_{0}\ge 3,\qquad \sum_{0}^{r_{0}-1}w_{j}=4,
$$

and $r_{0}=3$ gives the $WW$–type
$2,2,1$ for the black runs and $2,1,1$ for the white runs.  For that
type the man who sees the $WW$ block has the three unseen hats
$c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1}=1$ with three admissible completions and the
two spurious completions force a neighbour to know his hat already
after the first announcement.  Hence every $WW$–word is eliminated by
the second ``No''.  With no $WW$ run we have $r_{0}=r_{1}=4$ and,
$\sum w_{j}=4$, $w_{j}=1\;\forall j$, so that in $S_{2}$

* the four white hats are isolated,
* $r_{1}=4$, $\sum b_{j}=5$ gives the black run lengths $2,1,1,1$,
* there is exactly one $BB$ adjacency and no $WW$ adjacency.

Up to rotation and reflexion this is the almost alternating neck
lace

$$
W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B ,
\tag{2}
$$

i.e. in the normalisation

$$
c_{0}=0,\;c_{1}=1,\;c_{2}=0,\;c_{3}=1,\;c_{4}=0,\;c_{5}=1,\;
c_{6}=0,\;c_{7}=1,\;c_{8}=1,
$$

and every rotation of (2) is the same word.  In (2)

$$
s_{i}=1\iff i=1,3,5 ,\qquad s_{i}=2\ {\rm otherwise},
$$

so that $i=1,3,5$ are the three $W B W$ isolated blacks, $k_{i}=4$,
and $i=2,4,6$ are the three whites $B W B$ which sit between two
isolated blacks.  For a man $i$ let ${\cal W}_{i}\subset S_{2}$ be the
words of $S_{2}$ which agree with the six hats seen by $i$.  For the
three isolated blacks $i=1,3,5$ the view contains the $BB$ block
$7\!-\!8$, whence the three completions of the hidden triple
$c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1}=1$,

$$
(1,0,0),\;(0,1,0),\;(0,0,1),
$$

are reduced to the single completion $(0,1,0)$ by the requirement
``no $WW$ and exactly one $BB$''.  Hence

$$
c_{i}=1\qquad i=1,3,5,
$$

is common knowledge after the two ``No''s.  The two white neighbours
of the first two isolated blacks,

$$
i=2\ {\rm with}\ (c_{1},c_{2},c_{3})=(1,0,1),\qquad
i=4\ {\rm with}\ (c_{3},c_{4},c_{5})=(1,0,1),
$$

are forced to be white by the same $WW$/$BB$ elimination, whereas
the white $i=6$ which sits immediately before the $BB$ block and the
white $i=0$ which sits immediately after it still have the two
$ S_{2}$–completions

$$
(c_{5},c_{6},c_{7})=(1,0,1)\leftrightarrow(1,1,0),\qquad
(c_{8},c_{0},c_{1})=(1,0,1)\leftrightarrow(0,1,1),
$$

and the two $BB$–men $i=7,8$ still have the two completions
$(c_{6},c_{7},c_{8})=(0,1,1)\leftrightarrow(1,0,1)$.  Hence after the
common knowledge of the two successive ``No''s the five men

$$
i=1,2,3,4,5
$$

have a unique six-hat view in $S_{2}$: $i=1,3,5$ know that they are
the three isolated black hats $W B W$ and $i=2,4$ know that they are
the two whites $B W B$ which flank the first two isolated blacks.
Up to rotation these are the three $W B W$ men; in the usual
statement they are quoted as the three isolated black hats which are
the first to know that they are black.  The six remaining men, the
$BB$ pair $7\!-\!8$ and the white $0$ and $6$, still have two
compatible rotations of (2).

In particular the essentially unique distribution compatible with two
universal ``No''s and a ``Yes'' on the third question is the one $BB$
pair with the other three blacks isolated by the four whites, e.g.

$$
B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W
$$

clockwise, which is (2) up to rotation.  The three $W B W$ positions
are the three black hats which become common knowledge on the third
call; with the conventional counting of the five men whose six-hat
view is uniquely determined in $S_{2}$ this is five ``Yes'' answers,
three black and two white, the three black answers being the
customary three-Yes statement.  Any rotation or reflexion of
$W B W B W B W B B$ is the same necklace. ∎

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first universal No forces $s_i=c_{i-1}+c_i+c_{i+1}\in\{1,2\}$ for every $i$, no $000$ and no $111$ on the circle. $\sum s_i=15$ gives $\#\{s_i=1\}=3$, $\#\{s_i=2\}=6$, $k_i=5-s_i=4$ for the three $s_i=1$ seats and $k_i=3$ for the rest. No three consecutive hats are monochromatic.

Up to rotation/reflection the $5\!-\!4$ circular word with $s_i\in\{1,2\}$ is the almost-alternating word with four isolated whites and one $BB$ block, the remaining three blacks isolated $WBW$. Essentially unique up to rotation:

$W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\equiv B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W\equiv B\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W$.

In the normalisation $c_0=0,c_1=1,c_2=0,c_3=1,c_4=0,c_5=1,c_6=0,c_7=1,c_8=1$ we have $s_i=1$ for $i=1,3,5$ and $s_i=2$ otherwise. The three $s_i=1$ triples are the three isolated $WBW$ blacks.

The second universal No eliminates the $WW$–type. With a $WW$ pair two consecutive $s_i=1$’s would occur and a neighbour would have been forced on the second round. After the two Nos the only admissible completion of a weight-1 window is the central one. For $s_i=1$ the three completions $100,010,001$ are reduced by common knowledge that nobody knew on round 2 to the single $010$, i.e. $c_{i-1}=c_{i+1}=0$, $c_i=1$. Hence the three $s_i=1$ men know they sit on $WBW$ and are black.

The two black hats of the unique $BB$ block and the four whites still have a locally consistent rotation of the $BB$ block compatible with the two Nos, so their own colour is not forced by the public announcements alone. The three isolated black $WBW$ seats are the only seats with forced own colour on the third question.

In the $C_9$-orbit the views $V_0\equiv V_7$ and $V_6\equiv V_8$ remain ambiguous; the five seats $1,2,3,4,5$ in the normalisation have a unique six-hat view in the orbit, three blacks $1,3,5$ and two whites $2,4$. This is the source of the often quoted “five identifiable views”/“five black hats” counting. Strict individual epistemic knowledge gives three new Yes answers, the three isolated black hats $WBW$. Distribution up to rotation/reflection is one adjacent $BB$ pair, three isolated $B$’s separated by four isolated $W$’s, e.g. $BWBW B WBBW$, $BWBWBWBBW$, $BBWBWBWBW$. The minority $WW$-containing words such as $BWBWBBWWB$ are ruled out by the second No. Unresolved is the conventional phrasing of the count: 3 persons know their own hat, 5 seats have a unique view in the orbit.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first common No forces
$s_i=c_{i-1}+c_i+c_{i+1}\in\{1,2\}$ for every $i$,
$\sum s_i=15$, hence $\#\{s_i=1\}=3$, $\#\{s_i=2\}=6$.
So $k_i=5-s_i$ is $4$ for the three $s_i=1$ men and $3$ for the six $s_i=2$ men,
no $000$ and no $111$ on three consecutive seats.

Up to rotation the $5\!-\!4$ circular words with $s_i\in\{1,2\}$ are
* A : four whites isolated, black runs $1,1,1,2$, i.e. one $BB$ block and three
isolated $B$’s.  Modulo rotation/reflection
$W B W B W B W B B\equiv B W B W B W B B W\equiv B B W B W B W B W$.
$s_i=1$ is the three $W B W$ isolated black positions.
* B : a $WW$ block occurs, black runs $2,2,1$, white runs $2,1,1$.

Common knowledge of the second No eliminates type B. A $WW$ block forces a
neighbour to have a forced hat already after the first round, so the second
universal No rules it out. The surviving necklace is type A:
four isolated whites, one adjacent $BB$ pair, three isolated blacks $W B W$,
no $BBB$, no $WWW$. Up to rotation the normalisation can be taken as
$c=0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,1$ i.e. $W B W B W B W B B$, with
$s_i=1$ at the three isolated black sites $1,3,5$ and $s_i=2$ elsewhere.

For an $s_i=1$ man the three completions of weight $1$ are
$(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)$. The two end completions would make a neighbour
know his hat on the first/second round and are eliminated by the two
universal Nos. The only completion compatible with the common knowledge
$s_j\in\{1,2\}\;\forall j$ and with the second No is the central one
$c_{i-1}=c_{i+1}=0,\;c_i=1$, i.e. the $W B W$ neighbourhood.

Hence after two universal Nos the three $s_i=1$ men, the three isolated
$W B W$ black hats, know with certainty that they wear black. No other seat
has its own colour forced by the public information alone: the two blacks
in the unique $BB$ block and the adjacent whites still admit a second
rotation of the $BB$ block compatible with the same six-hat view and the two
Nos. In the usual phrasing these are the three new Yes answers on the third
announcement.

The $C_{9}$-orbit of the necklace gives five seats whose six-hat view is
unique up to rotation, viz. the three isolated blacks $W B W$ and the two
whites $B W B$ that flank the first two isolated blacks. That is the
five-identifiable-views counting quoted by several colleagues; the
essentially new knowledge produced by the third announcement is the three
$W B W$ black seats. Counting distinct own-colour knowledge the standard
statement is three Yes, three isolated black hats, the unique essentially
circular distribution being one $BB$ pair with the remaining three blacks
isolated between the four isolated whites, e.g. $B W B W B W B B W$ up to
rotation/reflection. The $B W B W B B W W B$ type with a $WW$ block is
incompatible with the second No and the $5$-Yes/4-Yes counts that rely on
it are discarded. The dispute in the round is exactly this three-Yes vs
five-unique-view counting; the own-colour forcing is three.

$0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,1\;$ i.e. $W B W B W B W B B\equiv

2.text:
With $c_{i}=1$ for $B$ and $c_{i}=0$ for $W$

$$s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1},\qquad k_{i}=5-s_{i}$$

is the number of black hats seen by $i$.  $i$ would know on the first
call iff $k_{i}=2$ or $5$, i.e. iff $s_{i}=0$ or $3$.  The first
universal No is therefore

$$1\le s_{i}\le 2\qquad\forall i ,
\qquad\sum_{i}s_{i}=3\sum_{i}c_{i}=15,$$

so that

$$\#\{s_{i}=1\}=3,\qquad\#\{s_{i}=2\}=6,
\qquad k_{i}=4\;{\rm on\;the\;three\;}s_{i}=1{\rm \;seats},$$

and no $000$ and no $111$ occurs on three consecutive seats.  The
second universal No kills the $WW$ type.  Up to rotation and reflexion
the only $5\!-\!4$ circular word with $s_{i}\in\{1,2\}$ and with no $WW$
run is the almost alternating necklace with one $BB$ block and four
isolated whites

$$0\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,1\equiv
W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B,
\tag{*}
$$

i.e. in cyclic order

$$B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W, $$

so that $i=1,3,5$ are the three $W\,B\,W$ isolated blacks and $k_{i}=4$
there.  For an $s_{i}=1$ man the three weight one completions of the
hidden triple are $100,010,001$.  The two end completions would have
made a neighbour know his hat already after the first round and are
eliminated by the first No; they would have made a neighbour know
already after the second round and are eliminated by the second No.
After the two successive universal Nos the only admissible completion
is

$c_{i-1}=0,\;c_{i}=1,\;c_{i+1}=0,$

i.e. the $W\,B\,W$ neighbourhood.  Hence after the two Nos the three
men who sit on an isolated black hat know with certainty that they are
black.  In $(*)$ they are $i=1,3,5$.  They are the three new pieces of
common knowledge on the third call, the usual three $W B W$ black
knowers.

12.text:
With $c_{i}=1$ for $B$, $c_{i}=0$ for $W$

$$
s_{i}=c_{i-1}+c_{i}+c_{i+1},\qquad k_{i}=5-s_{i},
 $$

$k_{i}$ is the number of black hats seen by $i$.  $i$ would know on
the first call iff $k_{i}=2$ or $5$, i.e. $s_{i}=0$ or $3$.  Hence

no $000$ and no $111$ occurs and

so with $a=\#\{s_{i}=1\}$

alternating necklace with one $BB$ block and four isolated whites,

triple are $100,010,001$.  The completions $100$ and $001$ make a

particular a word which can survive the first announcement has
exactly one adjacent $BB$ block, the four $W$’s are isolated and the
three remaining $B$’s are isolated $W B W$.

$s_{i}\in\{1,2\}$ and with the property that for every $i$ there are
two completions of the hidden triple $c_{i-1},c_{i},c_{i+1}$ of sum

$$

$$B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B\,W\equiv W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,W\,B\,B,$$

I’m still with the 3-Yes answer. Colleague 6’s \(V_i\) table is a nice observation, but it is exactly where the 5-Yes reading slips from “this six-hat string is unique in the completed necklace” to “the wearer can know his own hat.” The public information after two “No”s gives the one-\(BB\)-block necklace type, but not a public orientation of that necklace.

The three forced seats are the isolated \(W-B-W\) black hats. For those three, the hidden triple has sum \(1\), and the two alternative placements of that single black would have made a neighbor know on round 2, contradicting the second unanimous “No.” That is a genuine local deduction and does not require knowing which rotation of the final necklace is actual.

The two whites counted in the 5-Yes version are unique only after the \(BB\) block is pinned in a particular orientation relative to the observer. That is an external combinatorial fact about the representative, not the common-knowledge deduction available to the person at the table. C12’s “conventional counting” is precisely the overcount: it counts unique rows in the final necklace rather than people who can actually answer “Yes” on the third question.

So my answer remains: exactly **3** people replied “Yes,” and the distribution is, up to rotation/reflection, **B W B W B B W B W** — one adjacent \(BB\) pair and three isolated \(W-B-W\) black hats.
